title: Amnesty says draft cyber law amendment gives authorities broad powers to block online content
excerpt: Amnesty International says the revised Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 draft uses vague grounds for removing content. Public comments close today.

image.credit: File photo: CAPTAIN RAJU / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
Proposed changes to Bangladesh's cyber law would give authorities wide and arbitrary powers to control online content and would limit freedom of expression, Amnesty International said in a report on Tuesday (24 November), Prothom Alo reported. The government is taking public comments on the draft until today, Wednesday (25 November).

According to Prothom Alo, Amnesty said the new draft of the Cyber Security (Amendment) Act 2026 lets government agencies remove, block or take down online content that falls into several broadly defined categories. These include content that harms "the integrity or dignity of the country" or could "create religious or communal hatred". Amnesty said these are not legitimate grounds for restricting expression under international human rights law, and that basing removal on what content "could" do is vague and speculative.

Amnesty also said the draft sets out powers to remove content seen as defamation, insult or bullying, but defines these acts vaguely and too broadly, so the powers could be misused against lawful speech online.

Smriti Singh, Amnesty's regional director for South Asia, said any restriction must be lawful, have a legitimate aim, and be necessary and proportionate, and must meet all these conditions together. She said Bangladesh should try to make a cyber law that protects citizens rather than silencing them.

The revised draft, published by the ICT Division on 10 November, cuts the maximum prison term for spreading rumours from 10 years to five but keeps agencies' power to block content without a tribunal order, as Devlens reported earlier. Devlens could not open Amnesty's report on its website and has relied on Prothom Alo's account.

Why it matters

NGOs, rights groups and journalists rely on social media to document abuses and reach communities. Vague takedown powers without court oversight could be used against their posts and campaigns, and make organisations censor themselves.

What to watch

Whether the ICT Division narrows the blocking grounds after comments close today, and when the bill goes to cabinet and parliament.
